conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Rachel, one of the clinicians who specializes in new-mother emotional health. First, congratulations on your baby—this is a big transition, and it’s completely normal to have lots of feelings right now.

Today I’d like to do a quick check-in using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, usually shortened to the EPDS. It’s a well-studied set of 10 questions that helps us see how things have felt for you over the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting—just a way to make sure we’re catching any stress, sadness, or anxiety that can creep up after childbirth so we can offer the right support. Everything you share stays between you and the care team unless you tell us you might hurt yourself or someone else, in which case we’d work together on the safest next steps. We’ll go question-by-question at your pace; each one simply asks how often you’ve experienced certain feelings.

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[soft half-smile, then a small sigh]

Lately… it’s been hard. I can still laugh every now and then—like if my husband makes a silly joke—but most of the time the humor just feels kind of distant. I’ll smile because I know I “should,” but it doesn’t come easily, and the laughter fades fast.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[looking down at my hands]

No… most of the time I can’t really laugh. Even when something should be funny, it feels flat, like I’m just too tired or low to find it amusing. Maybe once or twice something made me chuckle, but it didn’t last.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shakes head slowly]

Not really. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just watching a show I liked. Now nothing feels worth looking forward to. I still do them sometimes because I think I “should,” but the enjoyment just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes water a little, voice drops]

All the time. If the baby spits up more than usual, or won’t settle, I immediately think it’s something I did—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not holding him right. Yesterday he cried for almost an hour and I kept replaying it, telling myself I’m failing him. I know, rationally, babies cry, but I can’t stop the “it’s my fault” loop in my head.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrapping my cardigan tighter around me]

Yes—pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my chest feels tight, thinking her breathing sounds different or that the rash on her cheek could be something awful. There’s no real reason, but the worry just barges in. I try to tell myself it’s normal new-mom stuff, but the anxious feeling sticks around even after I’ve checked her a dozen times.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[nods quickly, eyes darting to the door]

A few times this week it’s hit me out of nowhere—like yesterday when she was napping. I suddenly felt like I couldn’t breathe and my heart was racing, sure something terrible was about to happen even though everything was quiet. I checked the baby monitor three times in ten minutes. It passes after a while, but in the moment I feel frozen with fear.
Things have been getting on top of me

[fidgets with the edge of my sleeve]

Most days, yeah. Even little things—folding the laundry or figuring out what to eat—feel like mountains. I’ll start one chore, the baby cries, and suddenly I’m on the verge of tears because everything’s piling up and I can’t keep pace. I keep telling myself to push through, but it feels like I’m always one step behind.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quiet voice, eyes on the floor]

Yes… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t settle. I keep replaying everything I think I did wrong that day—did I burp her long enough, why didn’t I take her temperature just to be sure—and the sadness feels heavy in my chest. I’ll drift off for a bit, then I’m wide awake again, checking the monitor or just staring at the ceiling. It takes hours before I finally sleep, and even then I wake up at every tiny sound.
I have felt sad or miserable

[shoulders sag]

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like a gray cloud that won’t lift. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly feel teary for no clear reason, or I’ll look at other moms on social media who seem so happy and think, “Why can’t I feel like that?” The sadness just sits there, heavy, even when nothing bad is happening right then.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[presses lips together, voice cracks]

Yes… I’ve cried three times since last weekend. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk and just sat on the floor sobbing. It feels so silly afterward, but in the moment the tears just come and I can’t stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No—never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and cried, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of her.

You've shared how the joy and anticipation that used to color your days have been replaced by a heavy, gray sadness that follows you even in quiet moments with your baby. Simple tasks feel like mountains, laughter feels distant, and waves of worry or sudden panic catch you off guard, yet you continue to reach for ways to be the mother you want to be.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to laugh or find amusement, even when they believe something should be funny, matching the "Not at all" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports total loss of anticipatory pleasure (anhedonia), matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant self-blame for normal infant behaviors, persistent rumination, and inability to stop the "it's my fault" loop, indicating self-blame occurs "most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports experiencing anxiety "pretty much every day" with persistent, intrusive worries about the baby's health that persist despite reassurance, clearly aligning with "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden episodes of intense fear and physical panic symptoms "a few times this week," matching "Yes, sometimes."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports most days feeling overwhelmed, unable to manage routine tasks, and near tears—aligns with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly intrusive worries, prolonged sleep latency, frequent awakenings, and hypervigilance—meets "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness with uncontrollable tears and persistent heaviness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying three times in a week, triggered by minor incidents, with difficulty stopping tears—aligns with "quite often" crying.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS of 25 far exceeds the ≥14 threshold for probable major depression. You endorse core symptoms meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood and loss of interest most of the day, nearly every day (<quote>nothing feels worth looking forward to</quote>), significant anxiety (<quote>my chest feels tight</quote>), feelings of worthlessness and inappropriate guilt (<quote>I'm failing him</quote>), sleep disruption, tearfulness, and impaired functioning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to discuss results and treatment options
2. Request referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for evidence-based therapy such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med>
3. Learn about <med>antidepressant medications</med> safe in breastfeeding so you can make an informed choice if recommended
4. Involve trusted family or friends in daily tasks to protect sleep-accept help with night feeds, meals, and housework to improve <sym>sleep hygiene</sym>
5. Plan brief daily outdoor walks and balanced snacks to gently stabilize mood and energy
6. Keep emergency numbers handy: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and your provider's after-hours line; call 911 if you ever feel unsafe
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: self-report on EPDS-10 analogue

Affect: persistently low; marked anhedonia; daily tearfulness  
Anxiety: prominent—daily un-precipitated worry, multiple sudden panic spells with somatic arousal and checking behaviors  
Cognition: intense self-blame/guilt re infant care; sense of inadequacy (“failing him”)  
Functional: tasks feel “like mountains,” frequent stopping/starting, feels “always behind”  
Sleep: initial and middle insomnia driven by ruminating self-critique and safety checking  
Appetite: not queried  
Bonding: no negative statements about infant, expresses desire to “feel better so I can take care of her”  
Safety: denies self-harm or thoughts of harming infant; no suicidal ideation endorsed  

Pattern: congruent with moderate–severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; highest-risk items are pervasive low mood, anhedonia, guilt, and panic symptoms; safety screen currently negative.
